newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Britain's First Lady flourishes in first 100 days.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Britain's First Lady flourishes in first 100 days.

text.p: Her predecessor in Downing Street, Norma Major, wore a broad smile and advised fellow housewives to see sense and freeze leftover cheese.
The one before that -- a retired businessman called Thatcher -- appeared keener on golf and gin than the dry duties of life as a political spouse.
Little wonder, then, that Cherie Blair, wife of Britain's new Labour Prime Minister, is being treated like a film star.
Young, successful, smart and attractive, she has been a breath of fresh air in British politics during her first 100 days as the country's "first lady".
"Cherie is naturally brilliant. I have to work at everything," Tony Blair, Britain's youngest prime minister this century, enthused recently.
A husband's praise aside, Cherie is clearly a woman worth watching, as much for what she says about the changing face of Britain as about life in Downing Street.

She is a working mother with school-age children, and a tremendously successful one at that. Long the Blairs' primary bread-winner with a dynamic legal career, Cherie insists family comes first and takes pains to shield her offspring from the media.
"She's my role model," said her friend, the Australian novelist Kathy Lette. "She's one of the kid and career jugglers who doesn't drop things. She's amazing."
"Cherie is all my favourite F-words. Feminist, funny, friendly, fabulous. What a great role model for women as we approach the millennium."
Wary of strangers, she is quick to embrace loved ones -- and publicly -- in a country shy of showing affection. Her children seem to be rounded, regular people.

Her obvious glee and bear hug for Tony on the steps of 10, Downing Street after Labour's victory on May 1 exemplified how different Labour would be from the starchy Conservatives, personified by "grey" John Major.
KEEN INTEREST IN THE BLAIR FAMILY

While there is no official job for a political spouse in Britain, moves toward presidential-style politics and disillusionment with the royal family ensure keen interest in the Blair family, not just the top man.
After requests for privacy, the three children have largely been left alone. Cherie is a different matter altogether.
She has been portrayed as a reincarnation of Lady Macbeth or Britain's very own Hillary Rodham Clinton.

She was briefly dubbed "The Imelda Marcos of Islington" for her sizeable shoe collection and eyebrows were raised when a huge, hand-made Swedish bed was bought for the Blairs' new power-boudoir in 11, Downing Street -- the prime minister's residence was deemed too small.
Long criticised for lacking style, Cherie was then castigated for spending 2,000 pounds ($3,370) on a hairstylist during a high-profile U.S. trip.
Never mind that she paid for his services from her estimated 250,000 pound salary -- the desire to look good drew criticism.
Paradoxically, she was simultaneously branded too clever, too feminist, too leftist and too like the U.S. First Lady for some people's taste.

Like her U.S. counterpart, she follows politics closely -- Cherie signed up to the Labour Party as a teenager and ran unsuccessfully for parliament -- and is said to be more talented and left-wing than her husband.
But while Bill Clinton promised voters a two-for-one deal when he first ran for the presidency, Blair insisted the voters would only get one premier.
"Cherie has no desire for my job," he said.

When Blair won the election, Cherie Booth -- as she is known professionally -- carried on her own high-powered job, even arguing against the British government's line in a European gay rights case. She could be named a judge in a few years.
She is eloquent and persuasive in court, yet few Britons have even heard her speak. To most she remains an enigma -- but they know all about her outfits.

"When Tony Blair first became leader of the Labour Party, Cherie looked like wide-eyed terrified fawn. She was pictured endlessly in baggy clothes and an unflattering hairstyle," said columnist Lynda Lee-Potter.
With her elfin face, severe grin and starey eyes, Cherie has an arresting face. She does not photograph well and commentators made much of her ill-chosen suits, lupine smile and feathery hairdos.
Yet her decision to change all that and get fit and stylish attracted just as much criticism. In short, she was damned if she did and damned if she didn't.

Said Lee-Potter: "She lost two stones, began to go to the gym, took professional advice about her clothes and, above all, found a hairdresser she trusted. On public occasions she now looks svelte and stylish.
"I fail to see why anyone should object."

Indeed, none of the ugly stereotypes -- be it power-hungry wife, gauche sidekick or empty clothes horse -- has proved well-founded and Cherie has increasingly won plaudits for the way she has tackled her tricky job.
Mother, political wife, housekeeper and hot-shot lawyer, she has juggled her many roles well and the gaffes have been minor and mostly heart-warming.

The best came early one sunny May morning directly after her husband's landslide at the polls, when Cherie momentarily forgot her new-found status and opened the front door to a waiting, watching world.
As policemen stood guard, to no palpable effect, and the cameras clicked, Cherie froze: disoriented, bare-footed and wearing nothing but a short nightie.
With startled eyes and slept-in skin, she peered out from under an unruly bird's nest of hair, realising with a sinking heart that life had changed forever.
